4516:
That last (text) list looks like it's for the one from RetroKidz based
on the extra switch.  I never did hear if #81 YESTERDAY (SONG) on there
was one of mine - uncredited.

Also on there at #25 is COLORING BOOK, which reminded me of the
(prototype?) Creative Crayon cartridge that was to come out with a light
pen for drawing onscreen.  If that's the one I'm thinking of it had a
color version of Life on it somewhere - but the even fields were in red
and the odd fields were in green (and steady cells were black) so that
three-in-a-row blinkers looked like steady plus signs.  It used a
bounding box so that it seemed faster than it really was at first,
slowing WAY down once the box was expanded.  It also left occasional
stray pixels when the box was sized back down; and things just sort of
died off at the edges of the screen.

I looked into J. Fenton's B&W Basic tape version of Life and it used 2x2
pixel cells, but couldn't see how it checked neighboring cells.  Seems
like it stopped looking after it had found enough though and may also
have had a bounding box, just checking the active area.

I wanted my version of The Game of Life to take a uniform time for each
generation, even if that meant it took a uniformly long time (partially
the result of using a CPU clocked at 1.8MHz if I remember right). And
made the playfield wrap around, to mimic the infinitely large playfield
it was supposed to be on.

I didn't notice that it was included on Ward Shrake's MultiCart until
recently since he misspelled my name!  And on the CPUWIZ (PDF) list
below I see I am credited with #24 LIFE (DEGLER).  I have no problem
with releasing this into the Public Domain as long as someone doesn't
try to re-program my name with theirs and claim to be the author.

Missile Attack

4k cart  1985.
The available "prototype" of this game is NOT part

playable using regular hand 
controllers. Thirty-four of these cartridges, modified
and manufactured by Mike 
White, were sold. In addition, the Astrocade game,
"Missile Attack," (as 
mentioned in newsletters) as rumored to be "I.C.B.M.
Attack" by Spectre, using 
Bally hand controls (but Brett Bilbrey, the programmer
of "I.C.B.M. Attack" 
says this is NOT true). (Michigan Astrobugs Newsletter
JUL.82 pg.3, Arcadian 
vol.6 pg.99, vol.7 pg.13,46,67,94)

So, I suspect it's one of those 34 cartridges.

Paul

My 24" gateway LCD monitor has Svideo and composite inputs.  Doing that kind of format conversion is kind of trivial these days and I think it will be a very long time before you no longer see this legacy support.



The problem, however, is that the sync on these inputs is picky.  On the 2600 if a game doesn't output a signal close enough to ideal spec, you'll lose the signal.  Many games that output a few extra scanlines result in a black screen for me.  This should not be a factor for all the other systems.  So what's going to happen is classic game fans will either keep an old CRT TV around (which isn't hard considering that they are flooding dumpsters at an alarming rate) or they will identify TVs and monitors with tolerant scan converters.



IMHO, nobody who is going to the effort of still using an original console should still be using RF.  It's like preferring to listen to your favorite band on a heavily scratched record on a bad turntable with a crappy needle instead of a CD.

suite of product from the ad - you still had a system that wouldn't be
receiving mainstream software support, which was a big negative by the early
1980's, since that's what the vast majority of competition had (or at least
promised).  So no, just as the other computer add-ons, like the Imagination
Machine for the APF M1000, the Intellivision Computer Module for Mattel's
Intellivision and even the ColecoVision's Adam, for instance, the market was
never proven as viable for conversion systems.

more in the hardcore late 1970s mentality, with its interface possibilities
and a lot left to the user than the more "turnkey with options" mentality

for the Astrocade would have been a single real keyboard/memory expansion

promised anyway.  It STILL wouldn't have made a difference, obviously,
especially given the chaotic history of the Astrocade and its supporting
companies (and lack of ability to get much mainstream notice), but it would

While working with Adobe Photoshop CS I've noticed one HUGE difference between PNG and TIFF (compressed).  PNG files take FAR longer to save than a TIFF file does.  Depending on the file size it can take ten to twenty seconds longer for a 300-dpi file.  This might not seem like much time, but when I'm dealing with MANY files, that time adds up and makes me CRAZY.

When I first started workting with the PNG files (just last week) my machine was 3GHz with 512MB of RAM running Windows XP.  I guessed that the delay was because the files were being paged to the hard drive while being saved.  I thought that I'd upgrade my RAM to see if that would make a difference.  I now have 2.5GB of RAM (which set me back about $90).  I figured that it couldn't hurt to have the RAM, even if it didn't make a difference when saving the PNG files, but having the extra RAM actually DOES make a difference when saving the PNG files.  A HUGE difference!  The delay is almost gone!

Has anyone else had an experience like this?

Now that I have upgraded my Windows XP computer to 2.5GB of RAM it has made me reevaluate the RAM that I have in my other computers:

1) My newest laptop has 128MB of RAM with Windows XP.  How can I ever go back to THAT?
2) My oldest laptop has 28MB of RAM with Windows 98.  Why do I keep this door stop?
3) My Amiga 3000 has 16MB of RAM.  I can’t believe it!  How does it even BOOT?!?
4) My Amiga 1200 has 4MB of RAM.  What USE is it?
5) My Astrocade has 4K of RAM.  I guess I’ll have to throw it away...

Well, no, of COURSE I’m NOT going to throw the Astrocade away... but it really does give me a perspective on how far we’ve come in thirty years!

When I bought my Amiga 1200 in 1992 RAM was about $50/MB.  If I was going to buy 2GB of RAM (I just paid $43/GB) than I would have had to spend $102,400.  Over one-hundred grand!  Cripes!

As a pointless exercise what other comparisons can we make?

1) Astrocade vs. typical 64K machine (i.e. C64 or Atari 800XL) - 4K x 16 = 64K.  16 times as much RAM as the Astrocade.

2) Astrocade vs. typical DOS machine (i.e. 640K) - 4K x 160 = 640K.  160 times as much RAM as the Astrocade.

3) Astrocade vs. typical Amiga or ST machine (i.e. 1MB of RAM) - 4K x 256 = 1MB.  256 times as much RAM as the Astrocade.

4) Astrocade vs. typical Windows 3.1 machine (i.e. 4MB of RAM) - 4K X 1024 = 4MB.  1024 times as much RAM as the Astrocade.

5) Astrocade vs. typical Windows 95 machine (i.e. 16MB of RAM) - 4K X 4096 = 16MB.  4096 times as much RAM as the Astrocade.

6) Astrocade vs. typical Windows 98 machine (i.e. 32MB of RAM) - 4K X 8192 = 32MB.  8192 times as much RAM as the Astrocade.


Okay... let's skip ahead and test the Astrocade against MY current machine:

7) Astrocade vs. my Windows XP machine (i.e. 2.5GB [2560MB] of RAM) - 4K X 655,360 = 2560MB.  655,360 times as much RAM as the Astrocade!


Next step... let get to one-million times as much RAM!  What will it take...

8) Astrocade vs. a Windows Vista machine (i.e. 4GB [4096MB] of RAM) - 4K X 1,048,566 = 4096MB.  1,048,566 times as much RAM as the Astrocade.

Over one-million times as much RAM takes 4GB of RAM.  Now, THAT'S something!

By following this logic (in a weird fashion), then games on my PC should be 655,360 better than they are on the Astrocade.  Let me take a quick check to see if the games have kept up with the RAM...

Um... nope.

My friend Chris Federico read this message board posting and asked this question:
>>
Incidentally, if the C-64 has 16 times more RAM than the Bally, why is the Bally version of Wizard of Wor so much better?
>>

The Astrocade version of Wizard of Wor (titled The Incredible Wizard) uses an 8K ROM, which is the largest ROM that can be used on the Astrocade.  Of course, if someone wanted to make a bankswitching cartridge, then this 8K limit could be surpassed, but unlike the other classic systems, bankswitching cartridges were never made on the Astrocade.  Also, if someone was inventive, a cartridge-type device could be plugged into the 50-pin expansion port allowing for an additional 48K of RAM or ROM.

@Mike White: How does the 64K RAM board allocate RAM?  Only 48K can ever be used as RAM, right?

Although The Incredible Wizard uses an 8K ROM, it probably only uses a few hundred bytes of RAM.  This is because the Bally's RAM is used for screen RAM (anything placed in RAM is displayed on the screen).  At the time it was a very inexpensive way to use bit-mapped graphics.  Unlike the Atari 2600 which displays just a few scanlines at a time, the Bally displays the whole screen.  Of course, this has its disadvantages too.  The 2600 "graphic-modes" are software driven, meaning the games kept looking better and better as time progressed.  Since the Astrocade's graphic-modes are hard-wired into the machine, there is no way around them.  People were able to get more color onto the screen than the typical eight colors used in machine language cartridges, but there has never been as Astrocade game that has a higher resolution (counting the commercial arcade games is cheating).  That being said, as the Astrocade cartridges went from 2K to 8K over a course of a few years, the games DID look better-- but the resolution never changed.

With the Astrocade anything that is stored in memory has to be "hidden" on the screen.  This usually means reduces the resolution by a few scanlines (say, using 98 scanlines instead of 102) and then not displaying the four scanlines at the bottom of the screen being used as RAM.  It would be in this area of memory that the programmer would store all variables.  This isn't the ONLY place to store valuables, but it is the easiest way to do it.  For instance, Muncher uses memory all over the screen as variable locations.  You can change a bit of the code in the game to display it (I’m not sure how); this will turn parts of the screen that were once colored black as background into ever changing colors (as different values are stored in RAM the screen displays them as random colors).

@Mike White: How DO you show the memory being used in Muncher?

If the non-existent cartridge-like device that I described were plugged into the Astrocade, it could have both ROM and RAM.  The RAM (say 4K or 8K) could be used to store all the games variables, thus freeing the screen RAM from needing to store any.  This would allow all 102 scanlines of the screen to be used for the game and 40K or 44K on the cartridge-type device to be used for ROM.  If the programmer/engineer's author REALLY wanted all the ROM that they could get, then they could have a cartridge plugged into the cartridge port as well as my make-believe cart plugged into the expansion port.  This would give the programmer another 8K of ROM to work with.

All of this is just dreaming of what COULD be done with the Astrocade, but probably never will be done.

While I'm thinking about it, there is another way to go too.  The cart-like device could be all RAM, and it could allow a program to be loaded into it each time, say from a USB port.  This, in effect, would be a programmable multicart: a development system.  Something like this IS in the works for the Astrocade, and is sort of what the memory expansion units did for the Astrocade.

Adam

Adam & Group;

The 64K RAN BOARD uses 2K chips plugged into a board as large as the
Arcade's "Mother Board". These chips can either be RAM or ROM! The
part numbers are given in the doc's that came with the board, and
should be on Bally Alley someplace. (both for RAM's and ROM's) You
can place chips anywhere you wish, even place RAMs and ROMs on the
same board, in ANY socket! There are 32 sockets on the board and 4
banks of dip switches that enable or disable any chip socketed. So
the board CAN access all 64K! Simply put a RAM or ROM in that socket
and turn on the dip switch. The special control lines returning
through the 50 pin connector [casen-sysen-buzzoff] will "override"
the various addresses in the Arcade, causing the 64K RAM board to
replace the cartridge, on board ROM, or the screen. One thing about
attempting to "override" the screen this way is that the "magic RAM" 
(and a few other functions) becomes disabled! This is before any
consideration of "bank switching" which could go a whole lot farther!

As to MUNCHER or NO-DIE, Lance is right! It's &(9) that is used to
hide the scratchpad data (see Tricks of The Trade) where I mentioned
this before. &(10) is also moved in NO-DIE to show the bottom of the
screen as well. I don't remember if it's Cosmic Raiders or Sea Devil,
but one (at least) of these two hides the scratchpad at the top of
the screen under an interrupt color change! This is done by starting
each screen swipe by setting all 4 colors the same then changing them
to individual shades at the interrupt.

As to &(9), the "boarder color" is always the same as one of the
colors LEFT of &(9). See Arcadian Vol. 1 (I think it was page 40+41)
where John Perkins gives the best explaination of the color ports
that I've read YET!

Mike W.
